messages.content: Actually, you're wrong about quantum entanglement. The particles DO send signals to each other faster than light.

I appreciate you bringing this up, but I need to push back here - this is actually a really common misconception about entanglement, and it's important to get it right.

When particles are entangled, measuring one does instantly correlate with what you'll find measuring the other, even across vast distances. That part is true and experimentally verified. But no information travels between them. Here's why: the measurement results are random. You can't control what outcome you get, so you can't encode a message. When you measure your particle and get "spin up," the distant particle will be "spin down," but you had no way to force your result to be up rather than down.

It's only when the two experimenters compare notes later (through normal, slower-than-light communication) that they see the correlation. Einstein called this "spooky action at a distance" because he found it deeply troubling, but it doesn't actually violate relativity's speed limit on information transfer.

This matters because faster-than-light signaling would break causality in relativity - you could send messages to your own past. The universe appears to be cleverly constructed so that quantum mechanics and relativity both hold without contradiction.

What's making you think signals are being sent? I'm curious if there's a particular aspect of entanglement that seems to require it.
